response.passage: In geometry, we use axioms as self-evident truths that do not require proof, unlike theorems which must be logically derived. Consider two lines intersected by a transversal. If the interior angles on the same side of the transversal sum to less than 180 degrees, the lines will eventually meet on that side. This is a fundamental property of non-parallel lines. Now, look at a triangle with sides of any length. The sum of the three interior angles of any triangle is always exactly 180 degrees, regardless of the triangle's size or whether it contains an obtuse angle. Furthermore, when two straight lines intersect, the vertically opposite angles formed are always equal to each other, regardless of whether the lines are perpendicular or tilted. Finally, remember that complementary angles are simply two angles whose measures add up to 90 degrees; they do not need to be adjacent to each other to satisfy this definition. By applying these clear geometric rules, we can solve complex problems without relying on visual assumptions or misconceptions about how lines and angles behave in a plane.
response.summary: This passage explains that axioms are unproven truths and clarifies properties of lines, triangles, and angles. It emphasizes that geometric rules remain constant regardless of size, orientation, or adjacency.
